verses.note: The verses show sin's instinct to explain rather than confess. The rest of Scripture treats honest confession as the way back to God (Psalm 32:5, 1 John 1:9), exactly what neither the man nor the woman offers here.
God warns before he judges. The questions are an invitation to turn back while the choice is still open, the same pattern the prophets follow when they call Israel to do well before judgment falls.

Hebrews 12:17 says that Esau afterward sought the blessing with tears but ‘found no place for repentance’. Interpreters disagree whether the repentance he could not find was a change of mind in Isaac (so the blessing could be reversed) or genuine repentance in Esau himself. Either reading warns that some choices, once made, have consequences that tears alone do not undo.

Jacob does not say he is sorry, and the text does not put a confession in his mouth. What he does is return, under the name ‘gift’, something called by the very word he stole in chapter 27. The Old Testament's idea of turning back often takes this shape: a wrong not only regretted but repaired in kind.

Repentance here is concrete and communal. The household does not only feel differently about other gods; it hands them over, washes, and dresses differently. The same shape recurs at Sinai (Exodus 19:10) and in Israel's later renewals.

Judah's confession has the elements the Bible later looks for in repentance: he admits the fault publicly, names the specific wrong, and stops the behavior. The same man will later offer himself as a slave for Benjamin (44:33), which shows the confession was not a single moment of embarrassment.

The brothers do not blame Egypt, the famine, or their father. They name a specific wrong, a specific victim, and their own refusal to listen, which is how genuine repentance begins in Scripture, even before it is complete.

The steward's offer recreates the choice of Genesis 37: save yourselves and leave Rachel's son to slavery. Repentance is tested when the same door opens again, and the next verses show whether the brothers walk through it.
The brothers' return is the evidence the whole test was built to find. Twenty years earlier they left a brother to slavery and came home; now they refuse to go home without one.

Judah repeats his father's favoritism without complaint and repeats the story of Joseph's death without defending himself. The brothers' lie is exposed in Joseph's hearing by one of the men who told it.

For the first time the brothers name what they did to Joseph as pesha and chatta't, transgression and sin, and ask directly for forgiveness. Their confession in 42:21 was to one another; this one is made to the man they wronged.
Moses does not excuse the people; he names their stubbornness and includes himself (‘our iniquity’). The plea for forgiveness rests entirely on God's character, not on any promise of improvement.

The rite requires spoken confession. The goat does not carry away sins no one has named. Confession is built into the heart of Israel's most solemn ritual, which is why later Jewish teaching could insist that the day does not atone without repentance.

The people are not spectators of the priest's work. They fast and humble themselves while the rite is performed, so that God's provision is received by a people who acknowledge their need. Isaiah 58 later insists that such humbling must be joined to justice.

Ephraim asks God to turn him so that he can turn. Repentance in this verse is both God's gift and the person's act, and Christian traditions that stress grace (Augustine, the Reformers) and those that stress human response have both appealed to it. The shame of verse 19 is not the end of the confession; it is the sign that the discipline has done its work.

In this passage repentance follows the gift of a new heart; it does not earn it. The sequence is found also in Ezekiel 16:62-63, where God's atonement leads his people to remember and be silent from shame. Christian theology has debated whether repentance precedes or follows regeneration; this text places deep repentance after renewal.
